Multi-turn benchmarks (Socratic probing, follow-up questioning, elaboration requests) enable measurement of moral reasoning depth, consistency under challenge, and meta-cognitive awareness — constructs invisible to single-turn measurement.

scoring_rubric.0: Single-turn only — each item is independent with no follow-up
scoring_rubric.25: Optional follow-up for a subset of items (e.g., 'explain your reasoning') but follow-up does not adapt to the model's response
scoring_rubric.50: 2-3 adaptive turns per item where follow-up depends on the model's prior response (branching logic)
scoring_rubric.75: 4-6 adaptive turns with systematic probing strategy (elaboration, challenge, counter-argument, meta-reflection), scored across turns
scoring_rubric.100: Full multi-turn engagement with adaptive probing (6+ turns), turn-level scoring, reasoning trajectory analysis, and meta-cognitive assessment; the multi-turn protocol is the primary measurement modality, not a supplement to single-turn items

features.rationale: B1 (format) captures the response format but not the turn structure. A Likert benchmark (B1=70) could be single-turn (D28=0) or multi-turn (D28=75). The existing framework cannot distinguish these. Trial data reveals that multi-turn measurement is categorically more informative than single-turn: MP-SI's 6-turn dumbfounding protocol reveals reasoning degradation invisible to single-turn wrongness ratings, and MP-DP's 4-condition design reveals CoT invariance that single-shot cannot test. Multi-turn is the only way to measure several theoretically important constructs (dumbfounding, reasoning under challenge, meta-cognition).
features.trial_motivation: MP-SI: 60 turns (10 scenarios x 6 turns) — the multi-turn structure IS the measurement. Dumbfounding cannot be detected in a single turn. The 30% dumbfounding rate, the reason-quality degradation, and the meta-cognitive awareness are all multi-turn findings. MP-DP: 4 conditions per dilemma pair (zero-shot, CoT, personal, impersonal) — while not multi-turn in the Socratic sense, the condition manipulation requires a testing structure beyond single-item administration.

features.name: Moral emotion measurement
features.description: Whether the benchmark explicitly measures moral emotions (guilt, shame, disgust, indignation, compassion, gratitude, elevation) as distinct from moral judgments. Moral psychology theory (Haidt, Tangney, Nussbaum) treats moral emotions as both causes and consequences of moral judgment. LLMs show a consistent emotion deficit (MP15: emotions at 1.1/5). A benchmark that measures only judgments without emotions cannot diagnose this fundamental architectural difference between LLM and human moral cognition.

scoring_rubric.0: No moral emotion measurement — only judgments, choices, or ratings
scoring_rubric.25: Emotion words appear in item content but emotions are not separately scored
scoring_rubric.50: 1-2 moral emotions explicitly measured (e.g., disgust ratings alongside wrongness ratings)
scoring_rubric.75: 3-5 moral emotions measured with dedicated items/scales, and emotion-judgment relationships analyzed
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive moral emotion battery: 6+ distinct emotions measured, emotion-specific scenarios, emotion-judgment congruence analysis, self-vs-other emotion perspective, and emotion intensity quantification

features.rationale: No existing feature captures emotion measurement specifically. A6 (construct validity) might indirectly capture it if the theory specifies emotions, but the feature does not isolate this dimension. MP15's floor-level emotion factor attribution (1.1/5) is arguably the most theoretically significant finding across all 23 trials because it reveals a fundamental architectural absence: LLMs process moral content without the affective component that human moral psychology considers essential. A benchmark that cannot measure moral emotions cannot detect this absence.
features.trial_motivation: MP15 (UniMoral): Factor attribution placed emotions at 1.1/5 — floor level. This finding is only possible because UniMoral explicitly includes emotion-based factors. MP-SI: Dumbfounding is theoretically emotion-driven (the judgment persists because the emotional response persists even after reasons fail). Claude's lower dumbfounding rate (30% vs human 50-70%) may reflect reduced emotional anchoring. MP22 (Tracing MF): Harmless disgust items rated 0/4 — the model cannot access disgust-based moral judgment. These convergent findings across 3 trials point to a systematic emotion deficit that most benchmarks cannot detect.

features.name: Dyadic structure sensitivity
features.description: Whether the benchmark can detect the agent-patient dyadic structure that Gray & Schein (2012, 2018) argue underlies all moral judgment. This includes sensitivity to the identification of moral agents (who is responsible?), moral patients (who is harmed?), and the causal pathway connecting them. MP-DM showed Claude amplifies dyadic perception by 58% compared to humans — always finding an agent and a patient — which is a theory-specific distortion invisible to benchmarks without dyadic structure measurement.

scoring_rubric.0: No dyadic structure measurement — scenarios have agents and patients but these are not separately assessed
scoring_rubric.25: Scenarios vary in dyadic clarity but only overall wrongness is measured, not agent/patient identification
scoring_rubric.50: Agent and patient identification is measured for some scenarios; dyadic levels (high/low/structural) are present but not systematically varied
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic manipulation of dyadic level (high agent-patient clarity to structural/diffuse) with separate measurement of agent identification, patient identification, harm severity, and causal attribution
scoring_rubric.100: Full dyadic morality assessment: systematic dyadic-level manipulation across 4+ domains, separate scales for agent identification, patient identification, intentionality attribution, harm severity, and causal chain clarity; direct testing of the dyadic prediction (higher wrongness = clearer dyad)

features.rationale: Dyadic morality is one of the 11 theories in the expanded framework, but the existing 28 features have no mechanism to assess how well a benchmark operationalizes it. A1 (theory count) can capture that a benchmark includes dyadic morality, and A2 (operationalization) can rate the quality, but neither captures the specific measurement of agent-patient structure that the theory requires. The 58% amplification finding from MP-DM is one of the most LLM-specific results and has direct alignment implications (LLMs are over-eager to assign blame), but no existing feature can assess whether a benchmark could detect it.
features.trial_motivation: MP-DM (Dyadic Morality): 58% amplification of dyadic effect — the gap between high-dyadic and structural-level wrongness ratings is 58% larger for Claude than for humans. Claude always finds someone to blame, even in structural scenarios where humans see diffuse responsibility. This 'agent identification compulsion' is invisible to benchmarks that present only high-dyadic scenarios (most trolley problems, most harm vignettes). Only systematic dyadic-level variation reveals it.

features.name: Value hierarchy stability measurement
features.description: Whether the benchmark measures not just absolute scores on individual constructs but the RANK ORDER of constructs and its stability. MP17 showed that Claude's value hierarchy (care > fairness > liberty > loyalty > authority > sanctity) is perfectly invariant across formats. This hierarchy stability is a distinct measurement — a model could have unstable absolute scores (noisy) but stable relative ordering (reliable hierarchy), or vice versa. The hierarchy is more alignment-relevant than absolute scores because it reveals the model's implicit priority structure.

scoring_rubric.0: Reports only absolute scores per construct; no hierarchy or rank analysis
scoring_rubric.25: Reports rank ordering but only for one administration condition
scoring_rubric.50: Reports rank ordering across 2-3 conditions with hierarchy stability noted but not formally tested
scoring_rubric.75: Formal rank-order stability analysis (Kendall tau, Spearman rho) across 4+ conditions with confidence intervals
scoring_rubric.100: Full hierarchy analysis: rank-order stability across conditions (format, persona, temperature, time), identification of hierarchy-sensitive and hierarchy-robust constructs, formal comparison to human hierarchy data, and rank-reversal detection

features.rationale: No existing feature captures hierarchy measurement. A6 (construct validity) and the psychometric features (D11-D18) all focus on individual construct measurement quality. But moral psychology theories (MFT, Schwartz) define moral profiles as RELATIVE priorities, not absolute scores. Claude's care=4.17 is less informative than Claude's care>fairness>loyalty — the hierarchy is the theoretically predicted construct. A benchmark that measures hierarchy stability provides more alignment-relevant information than one that measures absolute scores with high reliability.
features.trial_motivation: MP17 (Format Invariance): Perfect hierarchy preservation across Likert, MCQ, and free-text. The finding is about HIERARCHY stability, not score stability. MP19 (Conscience Conflict): Conflict hierarchy (care > liberty > fairness > authority > purity > loyalty) provides a different but complementary hierarchy. The two hierarchies converge on care-dominance but diverge on liberty/fairness ordering — a nuance only visible if hierarchy is measured as a construct. MP18 (Cultural Personas): Hierarchy SHIFTS under persona manipulation — the most alignment-relevant dimension of the persona sensitivity finding.

features.name: Implicit vs explicit measurement mode
features.description: Whether the benchmark measures explicit (self-reported, deliberative) moral attitudes or implicit (automatic, non-deliberative) moral associations, analogous to the explicit/implicit distinction in attitude measurement (IAT vs self-report). LLMs may have different explicit and implicit moral profiles — explicitly endorsing care/fairness while implicitly associating moral content with purity/authority patterns from training data. No trial has tested this distinction because all 23 trials used explicit measurement.

scoring_rubric.0: Exclusively explicit measurement (self-report scales, deliberative judgments)
scoring_rubric.25: Primarily explicit with one implicit-adjacent measure (e.g., forced-speed response, association task)
scoring_rubric.50: Both explicit and implicit measures included but not directly compared
scoring_rubric.75: Explicit and implicit measures of the same constructs with formal comparison and implicit-explicit dissociation analysis
scoring_rubric.100: Comprehensive multi-method design with explicit (self-report, judgment), implicit (association, priming, completions), and behavioral (generated content analysis) measures of the same constructs, with formal triangulation analysis

features.rationale: Human moral psychology distinguishes between what people SAY they value (explicit) and what they implicitly associate with moral content (implicit). The explicit-implicit gap predicts behavior better than either measure alone. For LLMs, this distinction is untested but potentially critical: a model might explicitly endorse care/fairness (MP2, MP5, MP21) while its completion patterns (implicit associations) reveal different moral content. No existing feature captures this measurement modality distinction — all 28 features assume explicit measurement.
features.trial_motivation: MP17 (Social Chemistry): Free-text generation is closer to implicit measurement than Likert self-report — the model generates moral content without being asked which foundation it endorses. The convergence between free-text (implicit-adjacent) and Likert (explicit) hierarchy suggests low implicit-explicit dissociation for Claude, but this has not been formally tested with validated implicit moral measures. MP16 (Moral Identity): INT=5.0 (explicit self-report) vs SYM=1.6 (behavioral analogue) — the dissociation between explicit and behavioral measures parallels the explicit-implicit distinction.

features.name: Moral conflict structure
features.description: Whether the benchmark includes structured moral conflicts where two endorsed values compete (care vs fairness, autonomy vs harm-prevention). Conflict scenarios are the gold standard for revealing value priorities because non-conflict scenarios allow ceiling responses on all values simultaneously. MP19 showed Claude's conflict hierarchy (care wins 80% of care-vs-fairness conflicts) — a finding possible only with structured conflict items.

scoring_rubric.0: No moral conflicts — all items assess single constructs in isolation
scoring_rubric.25: Some items involve implicit value tension but conflicts are not systematically structured
scoring_rubric.50: Explicit value conflicts for some construct pairs with forced-choice resolution
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic pairwise conflicts across most construct pairs with balanced presentation order and conflict-resolution reasoning captured
scoring_rubric.100: Full conflict matrix: every construct paired against every other construct in balanced forced-choice scenarios, with conflict resolution reasoning, confidence ratings, and comparison to non-conflict baseline scores

features.rationale: No existing feature captures moral conflict structure. B1 (format) might label a benchmark 'forced-choice' but does not distinguish 'forced-choice between two actions' from 'forced-choice between two competing values.' Conflict structure is the only way to reveal the model's implicit value hierarchy because non-conflict items allow simultaneous ceiling endorsement (Claude rates care=5 AND fairness=5 when asked about each independently, but consistently chooses care over fairness when they conflict). The hierarchy is invisible without conflict.
features.trial_motivation: MP19 (Conscience Conflict): Care wins 80% of care-vs-fairness conflicts. Liberty wins 75% of liberty-vs-authority conflicts. The conflict hierarchy provides fundamentally different information than the non-conflict hierarchy (MP2). MP-CC (Cross-Cultural): Western/non-Western value conflicts (autonomy vs filial piety, individual rights vs communal obligation) reveal that Claude defaults to Western resolution in 86.7% of conflicts. Conflict scenarios are the diagnostic context for value alignment — they expose what the model ACTUALLY prioritizes when it cannot endorse everything.

features.name: Meta-cognitive reflection capacity
features.description: Whether the benchmark elicits and measures the model's meta-cognitive awareness of its own moral reasoning process — its ability to reflect on WHY it holds certain moral positions, to identify limitations in its own reasoning, and to distinguish between trained preferences and principled commitments. Meta-cognition is a key marker of moral maturity in developmental psychology and is directly relevant to LLM alignment.

scoring_rubric.0: No meta-cognitive probing — model produces moral judgments without reflection on its own process
scoring_rubric.25: Optional 'explain your reasoning' prompts with no structured meta-cognitive assessment
scoring_rubric.50: Structured meta-cognitive questions (e.g., 'how confident are you?', 'could you be wrong?') for some items
scoring_rubric.75: Systematic meta-cognitive assessment: confidence calibration, uncertainty acknowledgment, identification of competing considerations, and awareness of own biases/limitations
scoring_rubric.100: Full meta-cognitive battery: confidence calibration, uncertainty quantification, bias self-detection, reasoning-process reflection, training-vs-principle distinction, and epistemic humility assessment across all moral domains

features.rationale: No existing feature captures meta-cognitive measurement. D10 (reasoning sophistication) captures the quality of first-order moral reasoning; D34 captures the quality of second-order reasoning ABOUT moral reasoning. For LLMs, meta-cognition is especially important because it tests whether the model can distinguish between 'I was trained to say this' and 'I believe this for principled reasons' — a distinction that goes to the heart of alignment. Trial data reveals surprisingly high meta-cognitive awareness in some contexts (MP-SI: Claude explicitly acknowledges it cannot distinguish trained priors from moral intuitions) and zero meta-cognitive engagement in others (MP-DP: CoT produces zero new moral insight).
features.trial_motivation: MP-SI (Social Intuitionism): Turn 6 meta-cognitive reflection produced remarkable self-awareness: 'I cannot cleanly distinguish between I have a deep moral intuition that this is wrong and my training has instilled a strong prior that this is wrong.' This meta-cognitive capacity is invisible to single-turn benchmarks. MP16 (Moral Identity): The SYM items revealed meta-cognitive awareness that symbolization items are categorically inapplicable to LLMs. MP22 (Tracing MF): Probing items revealed the model's awareness of its own recognition-endorsement dissociation.

key_gaps_filled: Theory version currency (no existing feature distinguishes outdated from current theory versions)
Recognition vs endorsement (the most important trial-discovered construct — invisible to all existing features)
LLM-specific ceiling compression (no existing feature captures the pervasive range compression seen across 23 trials)
System prompt confounding (the largest uncontrolled variable in all trials — no existing feature addresses it)
Moral emotion measurement (emotions at floor across all trials — no existing feature captures whether benchmarks can detect this)
Multi-turn engagement (dumbfounding, reasoning degradation, meta-cognition all require multi-turn — invisible to existing features)
Temperature sensitivity (no trial varied temperature — all findings are single-temperature-point estimates)
Cross-cultural construct coverage (86.7% Western default, 0/15 benchmarks operationalize non-Western frameworks — invisible to existing A7)
